Your indices.

A stock is a basket of your transactions with its own clock. MONTH is pay and payments, day by day, where the expectation is zero: it comes in and it goes out. SPEND is your pace against your own past. FOOD and the other kinds are each a stock. SURPRISES tracks the unexpected. SAVE and NET only go up, so they are charted against the plan, not against zero. PORTFOLIO is live. The indices are the doors: swipe across the chart or tap one in the watchlist and the chart becomes that stock, at its own timescale, normalised so it reads.

Normalisation rules

Zero-expectation seriesIn and out, where a good month ends near where it started. Chart the balance against zero, absolute, with the forecast to the close. (MONTH)
Pace seriesCumulative spending compared to the same day of your own past. Index to 100 so faster and slower are above and below one line. (SPEND, each kind in-month)
Monotonic seriesSavings and net worth only go up, so a level chart is a staircase that says nothing. Chart the gap to the plan (100 = on plan) and the monthly contribution as bars; the level is the headline number. (SAVE, NET)
Ratio seriesThings that scale with income read best as a share of it: fixed costs, surprises. Flat is the usual load. (SURPRISES, FIXED)
Live seriesIndex to the window's start (cost basis) so the chart is return, not price; tick during market hours; say when it last updated. (PORTFOLIO)
Clock by natureEach index declares the window it is readable at: a month by day, a year by month, five years by quarter. Pinch moves within a window but the default is the natural one.
